heath_proof: For let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the fourth apotome AD; I say that the “side” of the area AB is minor. For let DG be the annex to AD; therefore AG, GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, AG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out, and the square on the whole AG is greater than the square on the annex DG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG, [X. Deff. III. 4] Since then the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG, therefore, if there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on DG and deficient by a square figure, it will divide it into incommensurable parts. [X. 18] Let then DG be bisected at E, let there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure, and let it be the rectangle AF, FG; therefore AF is incommensurable in length with FG. Let EH, FI, GK be drawn through E, F, G parallel to AC, BD. Since then AG is rational and commensurable in length with AC, therefore the whole AK is rational. [X. 19] Again, since DG is incommensurable in length with AC, and both are rational, therefore DK is medial. [X. 21] Again, since AF is incommensurable in length with FG, therefore AI is also incommensurable with FK. [VI. 1, X. 11] Now let the square LM be constructed equal to AI, and let there be subtracted NO equal to FK and about the same angle, the angle LPM. Therefore the squares LM, NO are about the same diameter. [VI. 26] Let PR be their diameter, and let the figure be drawn. Since then the rectangle AF, FG is equal to the square on EG, therefore, proportionally, as AF is to EG, so is EG to FG. [VI. 17] But, as AF is to EG, so is AI to EK, and, as EG is to FG, so is EK to FK; [VI. 1] therefore EK is a mean proportional between AI, FK. [V. 11] But MN is also a mean proportional between the squares LM, NO, and AI is equal to LM, and FK to NO; therefore EK is also equal to MN. But DH is equal to EK, and LO is equal to MN; therefore the whole DK is equal to the gnomon UVW and NO. Since, then, the whole AK is equal to the squares LM, NO, and, in these, DK is equal to the gnomon UVW and the square NO, therefore the remainder AB is equal to ST, that is, to the square on LN; therefore LN is the “side” of the area AB. I say that LN is the irrational straight line called minor. For, since AK is rational and is equal to the squares on LP, PN, therefore the sum of the squares on LP, PN is rational. Again, since DK is medial, and DK is equal to twice the rectangle LP, PN, therefore twice the rectangle LP, PN is medial. And, since AI was proved incommensurable with FK, therefore the square on LP is also incommensurable with the square on PN. Therefore LP, PN are straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational, but twice the rectangle contained by them medial. Therefore LN is the irrational straight line called minor; [X. 76] and it is the “side” of the area AB. Therefore the “side” of the area AB is minor.

10.94
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fourth apotome, the âsideâ of the area is minor.

**Step 1.** Let the area be contained by the rational straight line A and the fourth apotome BG, and let BG be divided at H so that BH is the whole and HG the annex. By the definition of a fourth apotome (D10.3.4), BH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A, the square on BH is greater than the square on HG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with BH, and BH and HG are commensurable in square only.

**Step 2.** Since sq(BH) > sq(HG) by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with BH, by 10.18 (applied to BH and HG), if we apply to BH a parallelogram equal to one-fourth of sq(HG) and deficient by a square figure, it divides BH into parts that are incommensurable in length.

**Step 3.** Bisect BH at E, so that BE = EH. Apply to BH a rectangle equal to one-fourth of sq(HG) and deficient by a square, producing segments BF and FH (where F lies between B and H). By Step 2, BF and FH are incommensurable in length. Since BH is bisected at E and divided unequally at F, by 2.5, the rectangle BF . FH together with sq(EF) equals sq(EH). But the rectangle BF . FH equals one-fourth of sq(HG), so sq(EH) = (1/4) sq(HG) + sq(EF), whence sq(EH) - sq(EF) = (1/4) sq(HG). Since BH = 2 EH and HG = 2 times the side whose square is (1/4) sq(HG), this yields sq(BH) - sq(HG) = 4 sq(EF), i.e., sq(BH) = sq(HG) + 4 sq(EF). Equivalently, sq(EH) > sq(EF).

**Step 4.** Since BH is commensurable in length with A (both rational), and BH = 2 EH, the line EH is also commensurable in length with A (for halving a rational line yields a rational line commensurable with A, by 10.15 and 10.12). Thus sq(EH) is commensurable with sq(A), i.e., sq(EH) is a rational area.

**Step 5.** Since BF and FH are incommensurable in length, BH (= BF + FH) is incommensurable in length with each of BF and FH by 10.16. But BH is rational and commensurable with A in length, so BF is incommensurable in length with A. The rectangle A . BF is therefore irrational, and the square equal to it (i.e., the square on a straight line we call s1) is irrational. Hence s1 is irrational.

**Step 6.** Similarly, since FH is incommensurable in length with BH and hence with A, the rectangle A . FH is irrational. The straight line s2, whose square equals the rectangle A . FH, is likewise irrational.

**Step 7.** Since BF is incommensurable in length with FH, by 10.11 the rectangle A . BF is incommensurable with the rectangle A . FH, i.e., sq(s1) is incommensurable with sq(s2). Therefore s1 and s2 are incommensurable in square.

**Step 8.** Now the total area A . BG = A . BH - A . HG (by 1.43 or the distributive property from 2.1 applied to the difference). Since BH and HG are rational and commensurable in square only, the rectangle BH . HG is irrational (by 10.21, since they are commensurable in square only and rational). The rectangle A . BH is rational (since A and BH are both rational and commensurable in length, by 10.19). Also, A . BG = A . BF - A . FG + (A . FH - ...). More precisely, the total area A . BG can be decomposed as follows.

**Step 9.** Consider the rectangle A . BH. By 2.5, since BH is bisected at E and cut at F, the rectangle BF . FH + sq(EF) = sq(EH), so BF . FH = sq(EH) - sq(EF). We set up lines so that sq(s1) = A . BF and sq(s2) = A . FH.

**Step 10.** We need to show sq(s1) + sq(s2) is rational and 2 rect(s1, s2) is medial. Now sq(s1) + sq(s2) = A . BF + A . FH = A . (BF + FH) = A . BH. Since both A and BH are rational and commensurable in length, A . BH is rational by 10.19. Hence sq(s1) + sq(s2) is rational.

**Step 11.** Next, consider 2 rect(s1, s2). We have sq(s1) . sq(s2) = (A . BF)(A . FH) = sq(A) . (BF . FH). But BF . FH = (1/4) sq(HG) by construction. So sq(s1) . sq(s2) = sq(A) . (1/4) sq(HG), meaning rect(s1, s2) = (1/2) A . HG (by 6.17 and properties of proportions). Thus 2 rect(s1, s2) = A . HG.

**Step 12.** We must show A . HG is medial. Since BH is commensurable in length with A, and HG is commensurable in square only with BH (by the definition of the fourth apotome), HG is commensurable in square only with A (by 10.13 and 10.12 — specifically, HG is incommensurable in length with BH and hence with A, but the square on HG is commensurable with the square on BH and hence rational). Therefore HG is rational (its square is rational) but incommensurable in length with A. By 10.21, the rectangle A . HG is irrational, and the square equal to it is irrational — the side of that square is medial. Hence A . HG is a medial area. Therefore 2 rect(s1, s2) is medial.

**Step 13.** Further, we show that sq(s1) + sq(s2) is incommensurable with 2 rect(s1, s2). We have sq(s1) + sq(s2) = A . BH and 2 rect(s1, s2) = A . HG. The ratio of A . BH to A . HG equals BH : HG (by 6.1). Since BH and HG are commensurable in square only, they are incommensurable in length, so the ratio BH : HG is not a ratio of number to number (by 10.7). Therefore A . BH is incommensurable with A . HG by 10.11, i.e., sq(s1) + sq(s2) is incommensurable with 2 rect(s1, s2).

**Step 14.** Now the "side" of the area A . BG is s1 - s2 (where s1 > s2, since BF > FH follows from the construction). We have established: s1 and s2 are incommensurable in square (Step 7); sq(s1) + sq(s2) is rational (Step 10); 2 rect(s1, s2) is medial (Step 12). By 10.76, the straight line s1 - s2 is the irrational line called minor.

**Step 15.** Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fourth apotome, the "side" of the area is minor. Q.E.D.
